content: Physical exercise is a well-recognized trigger for asthma symptoms and can cause bronchial obstruction even in individuals without a formal diagnosis of asthma. International asthma management guidelines recommend the use of beta2-agonists at all stages of the disease. However, there is no established consensus regarding the efficacy and safety of beta2-agonists for the prevention of exercise-induced asthma (EIA) or exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB). For the purposes of this review, both conditions are collectively referred to as EIA, regardless of the presence of an underlying chronic asthma diagnosis. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of inhaled short-acting beta2-agonists (SABA) and long-acting beta2-agonists (LABA), compared to placebo, in preventing EIA in both children and adults. The studies included in this review were identified through electronic searches of the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register of Trials and manual searches of respiratory journals and conference proceedings. The search was current as of August 2013. Only randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials that assessed the effects of inhaled beta2-agonists on EIA in adults and children were included. Studies that did not clearly define diagnostic criteria for EIA were excluded. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were used for data collection and analysis. A total of 53 trials involving 1139 participants were included. Of these, 48 studies employed a cross-over design, while five used a parallel-group design. Forty-five studies evaluated the effects of a single administration of beta2-agonists, and eight focused on long-term treatment. These two intervention regimens were analyzed as separate comparisons. For short-term administration, the primary outcome was the maximum fall in forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1). The data demonstrated a significant protective effect of both SABA and LABA compared to placebo, with a mean difference of -17.67% (95% confidence interval: -19.51% to -15.84%, P < 0.00001, based on 799 participants from 72 studies). Subgroup analysis revealed high heterogeneity in studies involving children, despite a comparable mean bronchoprotective effect between adults and children. Secondary outcomes assessing other pulmonary function parameters also confirmed a more favorable and protective effect of beta2-agonists compared to placebo. The occurrence of side effects was not significantly different between beta2-agonists and placebo. For long-term administration, the initial dose of beta2-agonists demonstrated a bronchoprotective effect. However, prolonged use of both SABA and LABA led to the development of tolerance and a reduction in the duration of the drug's effect, even after a short treatment period. The authors concluded that evidence of low to moderate quality supports the effectiveness and safety of single-dose administration of beta2-agonists, both SABA and LABA, in preventing EIA. However, regular long-term use of inhaled beta2-agonists induces tolerance and raises concerns about safety. This finding is clinically significant, particularly given the potential for prolonged use of beta2-agonists as monotherapy for EIA, despite warnings from regulatory agencies such as the FDA and EMA regarding the risks associated with LABA.
